title: Advent with Isaiah
hookLine: Advent's first readings come mostly from Isaiah: a people that walked in darkness

cards: Sit in a pew on a weekday in early Advent and listen to the first reading. Day after day it opens the same way: a reading from the book of the prophet Isaiah. Swords beaten into plowshares.
A wolf lying down with a lamb. A shoot from a stump. The desert blooming.
Isaiah is the voice the Church hands Advent, so much that some people call him the Advent prophet. And the Isaiah line the Church saves for Christmas night is about people in the dark.

teach.b: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the days of King Ahaz and King Hezekiah.

His world was frightening: Assyria, the great power of the day, was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah, and Isaiah names the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up by the Sea of Galilee, as the ones brought low.

teach.h: A GREAT LIGHT, IN THE PAST TENSE.
teach.b: Into that darkness he speaks in the past tense, as if the rescue had already happened. The Douay-Rheims reads: "The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light."
Light is risen, he says, on those in the region of the shadow of death.

teach.h: A CHILD, A SON, A PRINCE OF PEACE.
teach.b: Then a child: a son is given, the government will rest on his shoulder, and his names pile up, ending with Prince of Peace.
Jewish readers place this in Isaiah's own time, and some Jewish commentators have understood the child as a king of Judah, Hezekiah.
Christians read it as well as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, and Matthew's Gospel quotes the darkness-and-light line when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the very region Isaiah named.
Both readings live with the same words. Why give Isaiah to Advent? Because Advent is about waiting in the dark without pretending it's already bright.
Isaiah never says the darkness is small. He says a light shows up inside it.
And Catholics hear this passage at the Mass during the night of Christmas, so Advent's prophet gets the first word of Christmas too.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS.
teach.b: In early December the northern nights keep getting longer, and the readings answer with one stubborn sentence.

how: Through Advent, the first reading at Mass is very often from Isaiah, and Isaiah 9 is read at the Mass during the night of Christmas.

games.q: you're Isaiah. Assyria has just swallowed the northern lands, and the people are terrified. how do you speak?
o: tell them the danger is smaller than it looks.
speak of the light as if it has already come.
tell them to flee south and say nothing more.
games.why: he doesn't shrink the darkness. he says, in the past tense, that a great light has already risen inside it.

practice: If you have a Bible nearby, find Isaiah 9:2; if not, hold the line you just heard, the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.

Bring to mind one dark place you know, in your own life or in the news, and without fixing it, let the sentence sit beside it. If you pray, hold that place up in the light; if not, simply keep both in view.

wordCard.voice: Hezekiah, a king of Judah. Isaiah's child oracle, read by Jewish tradition as this king, and by Christians as a promise fulfilled in Jesus. Today's word.
